The claim that social media use causes depression and anxiety in teenagers is highly disputed among psychologists, epidemiologists, and social scientists. While there is a documented correlation between high social media use and poorer mental health outcomes in some adolescents, establishing a direct causal relationship remains a subject of intense scientific debate. 

On one side of the debate, researchers like Jonathan Haidt argue that the rapid rise of smartphones and social media in the early 2010s causally contributed to a global epidemic of teen mental illness, pointing to some experimental and longitudinal evidence. On the other side, researchers such as Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski argue that the vast majority of existing data is correlational, and meta-analyses suggest that the overall statistical effect size of social media on teen well-being is extremely small (accounting for less than 1% of the variance, comparable to minor daily variables like eating potatoes). Furthermore, the direction of causality is unclear (e.g., depressed teens may turn to social media for coping), and impacts vary widely depending on whether usage is passive (scrolling) or active (socializing), as well as individual vulnerabilities. Because there is no scientific consensus on causation, the claim is classified as disputed.
title: Social media causes depression in teenagers
